blocks.title: Student Learning Outcomes [C-12-D-79 to C-12-D-97]
blocks.text:
Part 1: Amines - Fundamentals and Classification
• Define primary and secondary amines, and explain their basic properties and reactivity.
• Identify the differences between primary and secondary amines in terms of their structure and chemical properties.
• Define the basicity of aqueous solutions of amines.
Part 2: Synthesis of Amines and Related Nitriles
• Describe the reactions by which nitriles can be produced: reaction of a halogenoalkane with KCN in ethanol and heat.
• Recall the reactions by which hydroxy nitriles can be produced: the reaction of aldehydes and ketones with HCN, KCN as catalyst, and heat.
• Describe the hydrolysis of nitriles with dilute acid or dilute alkali followed by acidification.
• Describe the preparation methods of primary and secondary amines, including nucleophilic substitution reactions and reduction of nitro compounds.
• Recall the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which primary and secondary amines are produced: a) reaction of halogenoalkanes with NH₃ in ethanol heated under pressure; b) reaction of halogenoalkanes with primary amines in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube / under pressure. c) The reduction of amides with LiAlH₄; d) The reduction of nitriles with LiAlH₄ or H₂ / Ni.
Part 3: Phenylamine and Azo Compounds (Aromatic Amines)
• Explain the relative basicity of aqueous ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine.
• Explain the properties and reactivity of phenylamine and azo compounds, including their use as dyes and pigments.
• Define the reaction of phenylamine with Br₂(aq) at room temperature.
• Define the reaction of phenylamine with HNO₂ or NaNO₂ and dilute acid below 1°C to produce the diazonium salt; further warming of the diazonium salt with H₂O to give phenol.
• Identify the properties of azo compounds (some examples include: a) Describe the coupling of benzene-diazonium chloride with phenol in NaOH(aq) to form an azo compound; b) Identify the azo group; c) State that azo compounds are often used as dyes; d) Recognize that other azo dyes can be formed via a similar route).
Part 4: Amides and Amino Acids
• Identify the reactions (reagents and conditions) by which amides are produced (some examples include: a) The reaction between ammonia and an acyl chloride at room temperature; b) The reaction between a primary amine and an acyl chloride at room temperature).
• Describe the reactions of amides (some examples include: a) Hydrolysis with aqueous alkali or aqueous acid; b) The reduction of the CO group in amides with LiAlH₄ to form an amine).
• Explain why amides are much weaker bases than amines.
• Describe the acid / base properties of amino acids and the formation of zwitterions.
• Describe the formation of amide (peptide) bonds between amino acids to give di- and tripeptides.
• Predict the results of electrophoresis on mixtures of amino acids and dipeptides at varying pHs.

blocks.text: Organic nitrogen compounds are essential to life and the modern world. They form the basis of life in the form of amino acids and nucleotides, making the most vital compounds for life, i.e. proteins. Amines and nitro compounds have the pivotal significance in the dye industry and medicines. Nylon, Kevlar®, and polyurethane are the nitrogen containing polymers, which are found in every home and office. Apart from these, nitrogen compounds are also part of our food, fertilisers, explosives, etc.

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Caffeine in coffee and theobromine in chocolate both are organic nitrogen compounds. These are active compounds that make our mood happy. What is the difference between these two?

blocks.alt: One row as printed: coffee beans; the caffeine structure (a six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring, two C=O groups, CH3 on three ring nitrogens and C-H between the two nitrogens of the five-membered ring); a broken bar of chocolate; the theobromine structure (the same rings, with H instead of CH3 on the left-hand nitrogen).
blocks.caption: Caffeine and theobromine, with coffee beans and chocolate (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure and photographs on PDF page 119).

blocks.text: Amines are considered as organic derivatives of ammonia, where alkyl or aryl groups may replace one, two or three hydrogen atoms of ammonia. The number of hydrogen atoms replaced by alky or aryl groups provides a foundation for the classification of amines as primary, secondary and tertiary amines. In the primary amines one alky or aryl group is attached to -NH₂ group. In IUPAC nomenclature system, amines are referred to as alkanamines.

blocks.alt: Primary amines in one row: CH3-NH2 labelled methanamine, CH3-CH2-NH2 labelled ethanamine, CH3-CH2-CH2-NH2 labelled propan-1-amine, and a benzene ring with NH2 labelled phenyl amine (aniline).
blocks.caption: Primary amines: methanamine, ethanamine, propan-1-amine and phenyl amine (aniline) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

blocks.text: In secondary amines, two alky or aryl groups are attached to NH group e.g.

blocks.alt: Secondary amines in one row: CH3-NH-CH3 labelled N-methylmethanamine, CH3-NH-CH2-CH3 labelled N-methylethanamine, and two benzene rings joined through NH labelled diphenyl amine.
blocks.caption: Secondary amines: N-methylmethanamine, N-methylethanamine and diphenyl amine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the secondary amines as CH₃–NH₂–CH₃ and CH₃–NH₂–CH₂–CH₃; a nitrogen bonded to two carbon groups carries only one H (–NH–), as drawn above.
In tertiary amines, three alkyl or aryl groups are attached to the same nitrogen atom e.g.

blocks.alt: Tertiary amines: N,N-dimethylmethanamine drawn with three CH3 groups on N (one above, one either side), and triphenylamine, an N atom joined to three benzene rings.
blocks.caption: Tertiary amines: N,N-dimethylmethanamine and triphenylamine (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 119).

blocks.text: Tetra-substituted nitrogen derivatives are also known, and are termed as quaternary ammonium salts e.g.

blocks.alt: Tetramethylammonium chloride: a nitrogen atom with four CH3 groups (above, below, left and right) inside square brackets with a + charge outside the bracket, followed by Cl-.
blocks.caption: Tetramethylammonium chloride, a quaternary ammonium salt (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 120).

blocks.text: It is important to note that the branching takes place at the nitrogen atom, rather than at the carbon atom attached to it, that determines whether an amine is primary, secondary or tertiary. This is not the same as in the case of the alcohols or monohaloalkanes (alkyl halides).

blocks.prompt:
a) Give IUPAC names of the following compounds.
i) CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂
ii) CH₃–CH₂–CH(NH)–CH₃ (note: likely intended to be NH₂ for 2-butanamine)
iii) CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₂–CH₃)–CH(CH₂–CH₃)–NH–CH₂–CH₃
blocks.explanation:
i) 4-methylpentan-1-amine
ii) butan-2-amine (the book itself notes that NH₂ is meant here)
iii) N,4-diethylhexan-3-amine (the longest chain through the carbon carrying N has six carbons)

blocks.prompt:
b) Draw a structure corresponding to each amine.
i) 2,4 dimethylhexan-3-amine
ii) N-methylpentan-1-amine
iii) 2-methylcyclohexan-1-amine
iv) N,N-dimethylethanamine
blocks.explanation:
i) CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(NH₂)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃
ii) CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂NHCH₃
iii) a cyclohexane ring with NH₂ on C1 and CH₃ on the next carbon (C2)
iv) CH₃CH₂N(CH₃)₂

answer_figure.alt: Structural formulas of four amines: (i) 2,4-dimethylhexan-3-amine CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(NH2)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3; (ii) N-methylpentan-1-amine CH3-(CH2)4-NH-CH3; (iii) 2-methylcyclohexan-1-amine, a six-cornered ring with NH2 at corner 1 and CH3 at corner 2; (iv) N,N-dimethylethanamine CH3-CH2-N(CH3)-CH3.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: structural formulas of 2,4-dimethylhexan-3-amine, N-methylpentan-1-amine, 2-methylcyclohexan-1-amine and N,N-dimethylethanamine.
answer_figure.long_description: The first structure is a six-carbon chain with NH₂ on carbon 3 (above) and CH₃ branches on carbons 2 and 4 (below). In the second, NH is joined to the last carbon of a five-carbon chain and carries one CH₃ (N-methyl). The third is a six-carbon ring with NH₂ at corner 1 and CH₃ at the neighbouring corner 2. In the fourth, an ethyl group (CH₃–CH₂–) is joined to nitrogen, which carries two CH₃ groups (N,N-dimethyl).
